# Variational method

We will consider the variational method in this chapter. For a hamiltonian $H$,
we define an energy functional
$$
E[\phi] = \frac{\braket{\phi|H|\phi}}{\braket{\phi|\phi}}.
$$ {#eq-vm1}
and find a $\phi$ that minimises it. That is, we find $\ket{\phi}$ for which
$$
\delta E = 0.
$$ {#eq-vm2}
It is convenient to write @eq-vm1 as $E[\phi]\braket{\phi|\phi} = \braket{\phi|
H|\phi}$ and find its first variation as
$$
\delta E \braket{\phi|\phi} + E\braket{\delta\phi|\phi} + 
E\braket{\phi|\delta\phi} = \braket{\delta\phi|H|\phi} + 
\braket{\phi|H|\delta\phi}.
$$
Using the condition @eq-vm2 for extermum we get
$$
\braket{\delta\phi|H - E|\phi} + \braket{\phi|H - E|\delta\phi} = 0.
$$ {#eq-vm3}
Since $H$ is hermitian and $E$ is real, $\braket{\phi|H - E|\delta\phi} = 
\braket{\delta\phi|H - E|\phi}^\ast$. Therefore, @eq-vm3 gives
$$
\Re\braket{\delta\phi|H - E|\phi} = 0.
$$ {#eq-vm4}
If this is true for every variation $\delta\phi$, we must have
$$
(H - E[\phi])\ket{\phi} = 0.
$$ {#eq-vm5}
Thus a ket that extremises the energy function is an eigenket of $H$. 
Conversely, if $\phi$ is an eigenket of $H$ then @eq-vm3 is satisfied for some
number $E = E[\phi]$ and hence $\delta E = 0$. This might make us feel that the
solution of the variational problem will gives us the exact eigenket. That is
not a correct interpretation. $\ket{\phi}$ is an approximation to the true
eigenstate such that the eigenvalue correspondint to $\ket{\phi}$ differs from
the true eigenvalue by a quantity that is second order in $\ket{\delta\phi}$.

We will now show that $E[\phi]$ is an upper bound to the true ground state
eigenvalue of $H$. If $\{\ket{\psi_n}\}$ is an orthonormal set of eigenstates 
of $H$ then we can express
$$
\ket{\phi} = \sum_n a_n\ket{\psi_n}
$$
so that
$$
\braket{\phi|H|\phi} = \sum_{mn}a_m^\ast a_n E_n\delta_{mn} = 
\sum_n |a_n|^2 E_n
$$
and
$$
\braket{\phi|\phi} = \sum_n |a_n|^2.
$$
We, therefore, have
$$
E[\phi] - E_0 = \frac{\sum_n (E_n - E_0) |a_n|^2}{\sum_n|a_n|^2}.
$$
Since $E_n \ge E_0$ for all $n$, the right hand side is a non-negative number.
Therefore,
$$
E[\phi] \ge E_0.
$$ {#eq-vm6}

## Excited states
We usually work with a set of states $\{\ket{\chi_n}\}$ that are tractable 
enough to compute $\braket{\chi_m|H|\chi_n}$ and express $\ket{\phi}$ in terms
of them. Let
$$
\ket{\phi} = \sum_{n=1}^N a_n\ket{\chi_n}
$$ {#eq-vm7}
so that the energy functional of @eq-vm1 becomes
$$
E[\phi] = 
\frac{\sum_{mn}c_m^\ast c_n H_{mn}}{\sum_{mn}{c_m^\ast c_n\Delta_{mn}}},
$$ {#eq-vm8}
where 
$$
\begin{eqnarray*}
H_{mn} &=& \braket{\chi_m|H|\chi_n} \\
\Delta_{mn} &=& \braket{\chi_m|\chi_n}
\end{eqnarray*}
$$ {#eq-vm9}
The minimisation problem is now about finding $c_n$ for which $E[\phi]$ is an
extremum. Unlike the previous case where we calculated the functional 
derivative, in this case we calculate the partial derivative of $E$ with respect
to $c_n$ and its complex conjugate. Once again, it helps to cast @eq-vm8 as
$$
E[\phi]\sum_{mn}c_m^\ast c_n\Delta_{mn} - \sum_{mn}c_m^\ast c_n H_{mn} = 0.
$$ {#eq-vm10}
Differentiating with respect to $c_k^\ast$ gives,
$$
\sum_{n}c_n\left(E\Delta_{kn} - H_{kn}\right) = 0, k = 1, \ldots, N.
$$ {#eq-vm11}
and differentiating with respect to $c_k$ gives,
$$
\sum_{m}c_m^\ast\left(E\Delta_{mk} - H_{nk}\right) = 0, k = 1, \ldots, N.
$$ {#eq-vm12}
Equation @eq-vm12 is clearly the complex conjugate of @eq-vm11. Equations 
@eq-vm11 are a set of $N$ equations in $N$ unknowns. In these equations, $E$
is no longer the functional $E[\phi]$ but an as yet unknown constant $E$ that
depends on the coefficients $c_n$. Equations @eq-vm11 will have unique solutions
if and only if the
$$
\det(H_{nk} - E\Delta_{nk}) = 0.
$$ {#eq-vm13}
The hermiticity of $H$ and the symmetry of $\Delta_{nk}$ guarantee that the 
roots of this equation are real. They can be written in a sequence $E_0 \le 
\ldots E_{N-1}$ and are the upper bounds of the ground state and the $N-1$ 
excited states. For each $E_k$, we substitute it in @eq-vm11 to get $c_n$,
which allows us to construct $\ket{\phi}$.
